title: Judge rules Los Angeles top federal prosecutor is serving unlawfully - Whatfinger News Quick Hits
text:
A federal judge ruled that Los Angeles’s top federal prosecutor is serving past legal limits as a de facto U.S. attorney, a finding the Justice Department is fighting on appeal.
The Hill reported that U.S. District Judge J. Michael Seabright found Bill Essayli, First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California, is unlawfully holding the top prosecutor role in Los Angeles and is barred from taking part in or supervising cases.
The order does not take effect right away. It waits on the court’s ruling on the government’s motion for a stay pending appeal. Essayli said he keeps running the office while the fight moves higher.
Seabright, appointed by former President George W. Bush, wrote that Essayli “is unlawfully serving as a ‘de facto’ United States Attorney” and is “disqualified from participating in or supervising” cases. The judge also found the Department of Justice unlawfully delegated powers that kept Essayli in the post after the 120-day legal limit for acting U.S. attorneys.
“is unlawfully serving as a ‘de facto’ United States Attorney”
Essayli learned of the decision through the Los Angeles Times and said the office had expected it. He posted that the stay leaves his day-to-day authority intact and pointed to the Supreme Court as the final stop.
“Just so there’s no confusion, today’s order is stayed and has no immediate effect,”
He added that he remains First Assistant U.S. Attorney, continues running the office, and that the Supreme Court will ultimately decide the matter.
Essayli keeps the office open while the stay holds
Fox News reported Essayli’s sharper response to the bench: he respectfully disagrees with the order and says the president and the attorney general have every right to select supervisors inside the Justice Department. He said he looks forward to serving in his current role until the high court settles the question.
That stance fits the administration’s larger push to place trusted prosecutors in key districts without waiting on a stalled Senate confirmation pipeline. Essayli was appointed last year in an acting capacity. Former Attorney General Pam Bondi named him first assistant U.S. attorney before the 120-day clock ran out, a move the court later treated as an unlawful extension.
Defense attorney H. Dean Steward challenged Essayli’s authority in August and called the new order a win. Steward told the Times the Trump administration ignored the laws on U.S. attorney appointments and got caught in Los Angeles. He also claimed the administration violated the law “again and again” to install its choices as chief federal prosecutors. Those are the challenger’s words, not the court’s full holding.
“a victory for the rule of law and the U.S. Constitution.”
Steward’s rhetoric is familiar. Judges have already second-guessed similar interim and first-assistant arrangements in other districts, and defense lawyers are treating every adverse ruling as a systemic rebuke.
Parallel rulings hit other Trump-aligned prosecutors
Just The News noted the same pattern the Los Angeles order cited: Essayli’s appointment was described as identical to that of Sigal Chattah in Nevada, whom the 9th Circuit found unlawfully appointed. An appeals court ruled in December that Alina Habba was unlawfully appointed as New Jersey’s top prosecutor. In January another federal judge found Lindsey Halligan “may not serve” as U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia because of an unlawful appointment.
Seabright had already blocked Essayli from overseeing criminal cases after declaring in October 2025 that the prosecutor had stayed in the role longer than the law allowed. Tuesday’s written order widened that finding and tied it to the DOJ’s post-limit delegation. The government is seeking a stay so the office can keep functioning while the appeal runs.
Court fights over executive personnel are nothing new. A federal judge extended a freeze on separate Trump-related activity even while insisting the bench was not picking a political fight. The Essayli order lands in the same climate of tight judicial scrutiny of administration staffing.
Voter-roll enforcement sits in the background
Essayli has overseen a Justice Department legal fight with California officials over noncitizens on state voter rolls. The department has asked California counties to identify potential noncitizens among roughly 20,000 names on those rolls. Essayli described the DOJ request as “simple” and said election officials who refuse to comply will be held accountable.
That enforcement work is exactly why the appointment fight matters to voters who want clean rolls and equal rules. When a sitting first assistant is told he cannot supervise cases, the practical question is whether line prosecutors still have a clear chain of command while the appeal is pending.
National Review observed that a ruling against the Los Angeles U.S. attorney could cut both ways. Assistant U.S. attorneys draw their power to prosecute from the Justice Department and the attorney general, not solely from the presidentially appointed district U.S. attorney. In other words, the office’s day-to-day cases do not automatically collapse because one supervisor’s designation is under fire.
That legal reality undercuts claims of instant chaos. It also explains why Essayli can say, with a straight face, that he remains first assistant and keeps running the shop while the stay is in place.
Appointment limits meet presidential staffing power
The Washington Examiner reported the core mechanics: Essayli stayed on after the interim role ended when the 120-day limit expired, then continued through first-assistant and related designations without a fresh Senate-confirmed nomination. Seabright, sitting by designation, sided with the defendants who challenged the arrangement and disqualified Essayli from overseeing the contested matters.
The statute sets a clock on acting service for a reason. Congress wanted temporary fill-ins, not open-ended substitutes. At the same time, presidents of both parties have used first-assistant and special-attorney designations to keep offices staffed when the Senate moves slowly. The Trump administration is testing how far that tool reaches. Judges in Nevada, New Jersey, Virginia, and now Los Angeles have answered with a narrower reading.
Similar friction shows up elsewhere. A Brooklyn judge tossed a Trump DOJ case against New York City sanctuary rules, another example of district courts drawing hard lines against administration legal strategy. Those rulings do not erase the executive’s interest in putting its own people in charge of federal prosecutions.
Essayli’s defenders argue the president and attorney general retain the authority to choose Justice Department supervisors. His critics call the workarounds unlawful. Seabright’s order adopts the critics’ statutory view for the Central District of California and leaves the ultimate answer to the appellate courts and, as Essayli keeps saying, the Supreme Court.
Personnel control at Main Justice has been a live issue inside the administration as well. AG Blanche has said he will weigh the president’s views on prosecutions while insisting the department’s independence remains intact. That balance is harder to strike when district judges are disqualifying the supervisors the administration selected.
What the stay leaves in place
Until the court rules on the stay motion, Essayli’s public position is unchanged: he is still first assistant, still running the Los Angeles office, and still treating the order as paused. The disqualification covers participation and supervision in the challenged matters once it takes effect. Line assistants continue to draw charging power from the department itself.
The practical stakes are highest on the cases Essayli has been driving, including the voter-roll records fight with California. If supervisors keep cycling through acting titles and first-assistant labels, defense lawyers will keep filing the same challenge. If appellate courts reverse Seabright, the administration gains a clearer path to staff the 94 federal districts with prosecutors who will actually enforce federal law on immigration, elections, and street crime.
Other Trump DOJ matters have produced their own judicial whiplash. A federal judge rejected an effort to kill a Trump DOJ fraud case, a reminder that not every bench ruling runs against the department. The Essayli order is the opposite result on the appointments question, and it now joins the Chattah, Habba, and Halligan decisions as test cases for how long an acting or first-assistant designation can last.
Seabright’s order is stayed for now. Essayli is still at his desk. The Justice Department is appealing. The Supreme Court, not a single district judge, will have the last word on whether the president can keep trusted prosecutors in place when the Senate will not move. That is how constitutional appointment fights are supposed to end, not with a local disqualification that freezes an office midstream.
